title: Claire Cooper — Acuity Law on measuring ROI from CoCounsel, HighQ and Westlaw AI (part two)
pub: Talking Tech with Legal IT Insider (YouTube), hosted by Caroline Hill
author: Claire Cooper

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Acuity’s experience aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: AI has accelerated suitable workflows and improved client service, but those gains have not yet translated into verified financial returns. Its staged, in-domain product testing, attention to implementation effort and continued human review support selective deployment and operating-model adaptation rather than assumptions of general competence or automatic organisational value.

kp.k: Product convergence is changing Acuity's implementation strategy
kp.d: Cooper says planned additions to CoCounsel Core, including collaboration, client portals and due-diligence capabilities traditionally associated with HighQ, have prompted Acuity to reconsider its deployment strategy. These are described as product plans over the next year, not established capabilities. The firm is testing both products and balancing potential impact against implementation effort and teams' exposure to change.
qs: However, they're planning on developing both of these products over the next year.
some of the things that are inside H highQ will end up inside core.
core is going to have the ability to collaborate. It's going to have the ability to collaborate with clients.
the teams have had a lot of change

kp.k: HighQ returns remain unestablished pending own-document testing
kp.d: Cooper reports completing phase one using Thomson Reuters' HighQ instance, data and US documents. Acuity assessed legal accuracy, conciseness, output usability and workflow functionality through a scorecard. Phase two would use Acuity's own documents for side-by-side comparisons; she explicitly says ROI had not yet been established. The stated decision window is January, end of January or February 'next year,' without an unambiguous calendar year in the discussion.
qs: we've just completed phase one.
they were using US documents
we're going to go to phase two of testing, which is us using our documents and our information to be able to really do a side-by-side comparison.
we haven't been in a space of being able to really establish what does the ROI look like

kp.k: AI targets initial document-heavy due-diligence review
kp.d: Cooper describes HighQ's intended heavy-lift uses in corporate due diligence and commercial-contract review. In the specific workflow discussed, a due-diligence questionnaire guides analysis of data-room documents to identify missing documents, further information requirements and substantive document issues. She characterises this as the first step of due diligence, not the entire transaction process, and notes that questionnaires vary by client and matter.
qs: HighQ is essentially there to do that heavy lift work
You upload your kind of due diligence questionnaire.
spit out a kind of a review of what documents are missing, what additional information is required and actually run an analysis on the documents themselves as well for you.
So it's the very very first step of due diligence.

kp.k: Westlaw testing generated strong reported lawyer demand
kp.d: Cooper reports testing both Westlaw AI integrated with Core and the standalone Westlaw Edge offering. Lawyers preferred aspects of Edge's information handling but moved between the two. She describes a four-week trial in two phases, starting with no more than four people and subsequently involving participating litigation teams; the transcript inconsistently calls the expanded stage the 'second week.' Her evidence of acceptance is lawyers lobbying for the upgrade, rather than a reported quantitative adoption rate.
qs: they prefer how Weslaw Edge handles some of the information but they will flex between the two
they love it so much that they lobbyed for us to get this upgrade in particular once we'd run through the testing
it was four weeks split into two phases.
first two weeks was very very small test team of no more than four people

kp.k: ROI measurement creates additional demands on fee earners
kp.d: Cooper explains that the short, finite testing period was intended to limit fatigue amid other demands and competing priorities. Collecting ROI evidence depended on fee earners committing time to testing and reporting alongside normal work. Acuity therefore made the scorecard increasingly clickable, aiming for completion in no more than about two minutes.
qs: we were concerned or I was concerned about the teams getting fatigued because there have been a lot of asks this year.
the way that you do that is through the fee earners, right?
I wanted to make sure that in their minds it was going to be a very finite amount of time
ideally no more than kind of two minutes worth of their time to complete.

kp.k: Scorecards distinguish quality, time savings and billing context
kp.d: Cooper describes recording matter stage, ease of use, conciseness and accuracy, with quick ratings out of five, alongside task-time questions and chargeable status. The purpose is to distinguish chargeable time from unrecorded or written-off 'shadow time' and account for different pricing arrangements. The transcript repeats 'with the AI' in both time-comparison questions, so it does not cleanly state the baseline wording. No numerical savings results are supplied.
qs: the first piece of that is kind of segmenting where within the life cycle of the matter we're looking at.
Was it concise enough? Were we in a position where there was enough accuracy?
all of these are kind of marked out of five
how much time are we saving that's shadow time and often written off or doesn't even kind of end up inside the CRM and how much of it is chargeable.

kp.k: Knowledge benefits require measurement beyond conventional ROI
kp.d: Cooper says Acuity developed a separate knowledge scorecard to examine pre- and post-AI capability, including strategic analysis, learning and skill improvement. She presents reduced dependence on partners and fewer correction rounds as examples of 'shadow ROI' the firm is trying to understand, rather than quantified findings. Her argument is that a topline ROI calculation does not capture AI's full day-to-day value.
qs: we've now also got a knowledge scorecard which is separate to this kind of tracker that tries to develop ROI specifically.
the knowledge scorecard is trying to get a sense of where you were and where you are post AI
Are you feeling like you're more strategic? Have you learned something new?
we're trying to kind of understand and track that kind of shadow ROI, which are things like I no longer have to go to the partners for X and Y.

kp.k: Forecast returns will be checked through continuing surveys
kp.d: Cooper reports partner agreement that an upgrade would involve Westlaw use at specified points in the matter cycle and surveys throughout the year to track forecast ROI against subsequent experience. She predicts returns will be significantly higher than forecast because the initial assumptions use only minimum use cases. This is an expectation awaiting longitudinal tracking, not an established financial outcome.
qs: we had alignment with the partners that if we upgraded there was buy in that at set times within a matter cycle the fee owners would be utilizing the Westlaw piece
we'd also be surveying them throughout the year
track the ROI that we'd forecasted off the back of the data they'd already provided.
We actually think the ROI will be significantly higher because we've only asked for kind of a bare minimum use case throughout a matter life cycle

kp.k: Faster research and review improve reported client responsiveness
kp.d: Cooper reports hours saved, especially when responding to potential new clients, and says the internal hierarchy of checking work has sped up dramatically. She emphasises the client value of responsiveness and persuasiveness at the outset, while acknowledging that not all benefits are quantifiable. Her account retains senior review rather than claiming that AI output goes directly from juniors to clients.
qs: they've saved hours you know in particular for potential new clients where the turnaround at the beginning is very important.
not all of it's quantifiable, right? So but there's still significant value with it.
It's never just the junior that does the work and then it goes straight out.
that entire process has sped up dramatically and that for customers is huge.

kp.k: Pricing implications precede verified profitability figures
kp.d: Cooper maintains that time remains a useful baseline because lawyers, including those using fixed fees, still think in units. However, Acuity is seeking deeper financial analysis, including EBITDA, and she cannot yet verify the reported positive impact with a number. Pricing and client targeting are next steps already under discussion, not completed or quantified business-model changes.
qs: it's the foundation for how lawyers work.
the EBITDA is definitely something that we're trying to kind of tackle
I can definitely say for sure we've had a positive impact.
we're not in a stage yet of being able to kind of verify with a number.
pricing and the types of clients that we are pitching to and we have started to do that.

kp.k: AI could expand mid-tier firms' competitive capacity
kp.d: Cooper reports corporate-team colleagues saying Acuity previously lacked the depth of fee earners needed to pitch for work pursued at larger firms. She argues CoCounsel supplies additional effective capacity and could enable more ambitious pitches. The firm still needs confidence that it can deliver the relevant workload and turnover; her claim that this could be game-changing for mid-tier firms is explicitly conditional, not evidence of realised market-share gains or staffing reductions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Claire Cooper describes AI-assisted first-stage due diligence and predicts that expanding CoCounsel Core capabilities will change Acuity's choice of platform.
pts.d: Cooper describes HighQ's intended role as handling large document-review workloads, including corporate due diligence and commercial contracts. A due diligence questionnaire can guide analysis of a data room to identify missing documents, request additional information and review documents themselves. She reports planned collaboration, client-portal and due diligence capabilities in CoCounsel Core, which have already prompted Acuity to reconsider how much to build in HighQ. These are workflow capabilities and product-roadmap expectations, not demonstrated HighQ ROI results.

pts.k: Cooper reports substantial time savings and faster client service, including acceleration of the internal review process.
pts.d: Cooper says AI adoption has saved hours and sped up work that could previously take days, including the hierarchy of checking junior lawyers' work before delivery. She particularly identifies responsiveness to potential new clients as valuable. Her account describes augmentation of lawyers and faster human review, not elimination of checking or autonomous delivery of legal advice.

pts.k: Cooper argues that AI's value extends beyond recorded time savings to research access, analytical capability and potential reductions in internal support needs.
pts.d: She says AI makes information available that would otherwise require hours of research. Acuity is investigating additional benefits through a knowledge scorecard: whether lawyers become more strategic, learn new material, develop skills, need less partner assistance or require fewer correction rounds. These latter benefits are presented as dimensions to investigate and track, rather than established quantitative findings.

pts.k: Cooper reports positive business impact, predicts ROI above Acuity's initial forecast and identifies pricing as an unresolved next step.
pts.d: Cooper says the firm has experienced a positive impact but cannot yet verify its EBITDA-related impact with a number. She expects ROI to exceed the forecast derived from trial data because the forecast assumes only minimal use across a matter's lifecycle. Acuity distinguishes savings in chargeable work from unrecorded or written-off time and recognises that fixed-fee and other billing arrangements have different pricing implications. She does not announce a particular new fee model or quantify profit gains.

pts.k: Cooper predicts that CoCounsel can give mid-tier firms greater delivery capacity and enable them to compete for work previously constrained by staffing depth.
pts.d: Cooper characterises CoCounsel as supplying some of the capacity associated with a larger firm's bench of fee earners. Acuity is seeking confidence that this capacity can support larger or different client pitches and additional turnover. She conditionally describes this as game-changing for mid-tier firms, which may be able to implement changes faster than larger competitors. This is a competitive strategy and forecast, not evidence of already-won mandates or realised additional revenue.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Cooper's implementation experience and internal testing; the transcript supplies no numerical ROI, accuracy or time-saving results.
pts.d: HighQ phase one used Thomson Reuters' instance, documents and data, including US documents, with scorecards covering legal accuracy, conciseness and workflow usability. Testing with Acuity's own documents was still prospective, and Cooper explicitly says comparative ROI had not yet been established. Westlaw AI underwent a four-week trial, initially with no more than four testers and then a broader participating litigation group. Scorecards captured matter stage, usability, output quality, task duration and chargeability; Cooper also cites users lobbying for the upgrade as qualitative evidence of perceived value. The transcript describes an internal data-based forecast but does not disclose its figures, sample of completed tasks, financial assumptions or quantified outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Reported Westlaw and CoCounsel benefits are current; HighQ ROI, broader realised returns and competitive gains remain subject to testing, adoption and measurement.
pts.d: At interview, HighQ had completed phase one and was moving to phase two with Acuity's documents for side-by-side comparison. Cooper expected clarity on platform fit around the end of January or February 'next year' and described product development over the following year. Although the document is labelled 2026, the transcript does not independently establish a recording date, so those relative deadlines should be retained. Future ROI depends on agreed usage at specific matter stages and ongoing surveys. Platform selection must account for change fatigue, HighQ's greater configuration requirements and evolving Core capabilities. Larger-client ambitions depend on confidence in delivery capacity; mid-tier competitive gains are explicitly conditional.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern Acuity's lawyers, supervising partners, commercial clients and mid-tier firms competing with larger firms.
pts.d: Litigation fee earners are the principal Westlaw AI trial population; corporate teams are exploring due diligence and expanded pitching capacity. Lawyers may spend less time researching and gain analytical support, while partners may face fewer routine questions or correction rounds if the anticipated knowledge benefits materialise. Fee earners also bear the burden of testing and recording outcomes alongside client work. Existing and prospective clients may receive faster responses and reviewed work. Acuity's management must determine whether operational savings translate into financial returns and how pricing should change. The broader market prediction concerns mid-tier firms' ability to compete with larger staffing benches; Cooper makes no claim here about access to justice, profession-wide job losses or replacing partners or juniors.
